Remarks: [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Remarks: From their self-made mini-pools on the top of rocks surrounded by crustose corallines. [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Remarks: fleshy spines on girdle. [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Remarks: [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Remarks: [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Remarks: [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Determination: Nuttallina sp. A or N. fluxa
Remarks: low in Nuttallina zone; small, short gill row. [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]

Determination: Nuttallina sp. A or N. fluxa
Remarks: n. sp. A is being described by Piper MS. [Doug Eernisse — In vicinity of San Diego; there is a second less common species besides the ubiquitous N. fluxa, we call N. sp. A, which is smaller, lower in intertidal, narrower, has fewer gills per side, with each gill row only ~70% of pallial groove - described only in PhD dissertation at Scripps in 1984 by Steve Piper - DE is working with Steve to publish the species description. DE has had two grad students who have completed (Newton Hood) or in process of completing (Kenadee Zernickow) Masters theses involving Nuttallina sp. A. In central Calif., can be distinguished by its whitish spines, not dark as in N. californica. N. fluxa also has whitish spines but does not occur in central Calif. It is difficult to distinguish N. fluxa and N. sp. A in especially live specimens. N. fluxa has gill row ~75-80% of foot length & N. sp. A is < 75% of gill row. In preserved animals one can count the gills and that is diagnostic. I recommend "Nuttallina" The third species, N. californica, is very common north of Pt. Conception, is larger than other two spp., and (easiest) has dark girdle spines, gill row is ~100% of pallial groove length. It does occur in so cal at exposed headlands, e.g., Pt. Dume.]
